Plus, new AI features from Adobe MAX, big updates to Claude, and a rapid-fire roundup of everything else happening in AI.

items.transcript: This week has to be the wildest week I've ever experienced in the world of AI. The only thing that even comes remotely close was that one week when Sam Altman got fired and then rehired. We saw the two best new large language models the world has ever seen this week, and that's not even the biggest story [music] because it was all overshadowed by this Jensen Huang and Nvidia drama. Now, I doubt there's really anyone on the planet who hasn't [laughter] already heard this story and kind of been following along, but I'm going to give my quick recap here anyway. So, a few weeks ago, news came out that the US government believed that there was a Chinese spy who had infiltrated Nvidia. Not too long after that, it came out that this potential Chinese spy was actually in a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. Now, the woman who was believed to be a spy was someone by the name of Alice Huang, same last name, but no relation. Alice Huang was an executive for a company called MegaSpeed. Now, this MegaSpeed company has come under US scrutiny for smuggling advanced Nvidia chips into China. Now, this company is based in Singapore, but was seemingly an easy route to get these chips into Asia and then up into China. Now, up until this weekend, this was all just kind of speculation. We didn't know what the real truth was yet. Then over the weekend, on November 8th, Jensen sent this memo to all of his employees. I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. There's no excuse for what I did. I'm deeply sorry. Basically, a giant apology letter confirming that he had been unfaithful. He goes on to say regarding the national security concerns raised in the news report, Nvidia's board of directors has initiated an independent investigation. He'll cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I'm proud and grateful to be an American. Now, this wasn't any sort of confirmation that this affair was with Alice Huang, but that's what most people read into this. Now, I've seen of posts over on X and on other YouTube comments saying give Jensen a break. His infidelity shouldn't be a reason to push him out of the company. Everybody's making too big of a deal out of this. Yes, it's horrible for his wife and his family, but at the end of the day, he's done an excellent job at running this company. But the thing is, the reason everybody's upset and the reason he's under investigation and the reason he's ultimately gotten pushed out of NVIDIA was not because he had these affairs, but because of the potential result of this affair with Alice Huang. The information put out this report, how Jensen Huang's years-long ties to Alice Huang enabled $7 billion plus NVIDIA chip sales to China. The gist of it is that it is illegal to sell advanced chips to China. You can't do it. Now, NVIDIA had permission to sell like lower powered lesser chips to China, but not their like best of the best chips that the US companies had access to. Well, again, from all of the current information that we have, Mega Speed, the company that Alice Huang is at, is a Singapore registered company that US law enforcement has been reportedly probing for smuggling NVIDIA chips from Southeast Asia into China. Between 2023 and 2025, Mega Speed's NVIDIA imports totaled $4.6 billion. Now, some have been used in Southeast Asia, but others went to Century Litong. Now, Century Litong is a Chinese-based company founded in 2023. Some of the chips that Century Litong acquired eventually ended up in data centers serving Alibaba, Tencent, and smaller Chinese labs. So again, the issue isn't that he had these affairs. Yes, that sort of tells people where some of his morals lie, but at the end of the day, the real reason that everybody is upset about this was that one of these romantic relationships was with this woman who had ties to a company that was illegally importing chips into China. Now, things get even weirder here. When you look at Nvidia's reported geographic revenue for quarter by where they were shipping chips. Now, most of their chips were being shipped to USA. The blue is October, the gray is July. So, most of their chips in July were staying in the US and same with October. Back in July, the second largest importer of these chips was Singapore, but then in October, just, you know, last month, they just flat out stopped reporting how many chips they were selling to Singapore. They just left that information out. They apparently switched up their reporting methods. October 2025, Nvidia switched reporting methods. It began reporting geographic revenue based upon the location of the customer's headquarters rather than customer billing location as it had previously done. Under the former methodology, Nvidia's breakdown showed revenue from US, Singapore, Taiwan, China, and other. Under the new methodology, Nvidia stopped reporting revenue tied to Singapore and continued to show the other geographic lines. So, we can see that China stayed relatively the same, Taiwan got a big boost, and US got a big boost from July to October, and Singapore just now no longer shows any revenue. When you start to put these pieces together, you start to understand that, okay, maybe the affairs aren't really the big issue here. [laughter] Maybe the issues are he's figuring out ways to route chips into China or he's in a romantic relationship with somebody who's figuring out how to route chips into China and he's unaware that that's happening. But then the story continues to escalate. This starts to say more about his character than anything. Turns out that, you know, the one affair wasn't the only affair. On Wednesday, news came out that Jensen had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who directly reported to him. This was with someone named Kimberly Powell, who's Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Under Nvidia's code of conduct, employees are told to avoid situations where actions create conflict, including personal relationships. I think anybody can pretty quickly see why this is also a problem. Like, if somebody is your direct subordinate and you have a relationship with them, well, the dynamics of those relationships are always going to be called into question because, well, that was your subordinate. Now, there's nothing to imply that any of it was like non-consensual or anything like that, but it does show that Jensen was willing to go against like his own code of conduct that he set for his own company. And this all came to a head on Thursday, the day that I'm actually recording this video, where Nvidia announces a CEO transition. Jensen has officially stepped down and resigned. He will not be on the board. He will not be CEO. Colette Kress, who's the EVP and CFO, is the interim CEO. She likely won't be the long-term CEO, but she's filling that role for now. Now, everything points to the board asking Jensen to resign, which is most likely what happened. And then also on this same day, the day that Jensen officially resigned, another report came out about a second relationship with a different employee. Now, there's not a lot of details about this one yet, but according to people familiar, there was a second employee that he also had a relationship. So, if you're keeping count, that's three different affairs that we know of from Jensen. One with a woman who runs a Singaporean company who imports chips into China, and two with employees of Nvidia. Now, why is this such a big deal? I I think we have a pretty good understanding of why he stepped down and why the board would have wanted him to step down, but him actually stepping down feels just absolutely wild because he has been the CEO of this company for 33 years. He founded it himself. He worked at Denny's as a dishwasher while bootstrapping this company and then grew it to literally the largest company the world has ever seen. He got it up to a $5 trillion company at one point. And the company Nvidia is literally at the center of everything AI. Literally every company that does anything in AI touches NVIDIA in some way. They either buy their chips, they use their software, they train on their hardware. NVIDIA sells to everybody, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, all of these companies, literally name a company, they probably work with NVIDIA. The one major exception being Apple, but you know, we could see where Apple has currently landed in the AI race right now. So the once largest company in the world, it's now I think in third place after all of this drama, but the once largest company in the world who literally has their fingerprint on all of the AI that exists right now was led by one person who grew this company to what it is over 33 years and then overnight that person's gone. They're just pretty much not involved in the company anymore. That is a wild chain of events. Now I wouldn't be surprised if he steps aside, is quiet for three, six months, all of this sort of blows over and then NVIDIA begs him to come back if the stock is still struggling. I say maybe like 50/50 chance something like that happens because he is like the face, the voice of the AI revolution. He's been out there being the biggest sort of campaigner for both open source and less regulation on AI. Like he is out there being the spokesperson for why AI is important to our future and now he's probably just going to go silent for a while. Wild, wild chain of events. And I'll definitely keep up with this story and make sure I keep you informed as it goes on. But there is other news [laughter] that I want to talk about today, believe it or not. The next update is from OpenAI and it's their new Decisions API. Basically a lot of times when you use AI, you don't need it to like write out some long response for you. You just need it to make like a real quick decision. So here's a cool example. Imagine you're building an app that checks if like return packages are damaged. You give the Decisions API an image and it'll return a probability of whether or not there's damage, like a crack or a dent. Then your app can use that to flag the product for review. And in total, there's three different types of decisions this decision model can make. Predicate, which will give you a probability. Choice, which will pick from like a list of options. And score, which will rank something on like a scale. And these decisions can be up to 10 times faster than using the Responses API in GPT-6 Luna. It's also ridiculously cheap, just 10 cents per million uncached input tokens and like no output token charges. This can be used for things like organizing your email inbox, scoring how serious a technical issue is, or helping your agent decide whether or not to keep on going, retry something, or ask you for help. Check it out at the link in the description box, and thank you so much to OpenAI for sponsoring this portion of today's video. Now let's get back to it. This week saw the launch of the two new best models the world has ever seen, which is crazy to think about on this week with everything else that happened. So on November 9th, Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. And according to every benchmark, it is pretty much the best model the world has ever seen with a few outliers coming from Gemini 4 Carbon, which also officially got publicly released this week. Now Gemini 4 Carbon was announced a few weeks ago, but not made available to people. This week, Gemini 4 Carbon was made available to people. But let's stick on Claude Fable 5.2 for a second. I'm not going to go too deep into this because I did an entire breakdown video of this one. If you check out this video called Anthropic's Fable 5.2 is the world's best AI model, that breaks down all the details of Fable 5.1, but it's a really good model. I've been using it ever since it came out, and it's become my daily driver for most things. It's slightly cheaper than 5.1, but pretty much smarter than every other model out there When it comes to writing code, when it comes to design, when it comes to editing videos, it is just ultra solid. In my earlier video from earlier this week about the model, I tested it with my Mega Bonk test and it looked like this. I also, of course, ran it through Busi Bench. This was the Busi it generated. It did take almost 20 minutes and $5 to generate and landed number seventh on my LLM as a judge leaderboard. And then over on artificial analysis, this one sort of ranks the sort of objectively best models by combining a ton of different benchmarks. Claude Fable 5.2 is the best by a pretty big margin as well, a jump over Gemini 4 Carbon, the other model that came out this week. Now, it is the most expensive per task to run, but this is also being run on Max, which they actually recommend you run it on medium or high, so you're probably not going to see like this kind of cost out of it. Again, I did a much deeper breakdown, so check that video out to get more details. And like I mentioned, we also got Gemini 4 [snorts] Carbon, which the timing on this one is so interesting because Gemini 4 Carbon was announced a couple of weeks ago, and when they announced it back on October 28th, all of their leaderboards had this as the best model the world has ever seen. It crushed every single benchmark. Over on artificial analysis, it was in the number one spot at 60, beating out Opus 5.5 at the time. And well, Claude Fable 5.2 hadn't been launched yet. So they announced that they had made the best model anybody has ever seen. This is it. This is the model to beat. This is the new bar that we just set, but they didn't make it available to people. They said it's just for cybersecurity testers and a few, you know, trusted tester type people, but look at these benchmarks. It's the best. Well, then Fable 5.2 came along this week, dropped early in the week, and I think Google went, oh crap, they just beat us on everything. So Gemini 4 Carbon was made available the day after Fable 5.2 and was completely overshadowed by Fable. And as of now, is the second best model on the leaderboard. I will say, it is still a really, really good model though. Let's go ahead and jump into a game here. I would say that graphically it did a better job than what Fable 5.2 did. And yeah, I mean it seems to work. Everything you'd expect it to do works well. So if I'm being honest, I actually think this did a better job than Fable 5.2 did with the game. But you know, according to the benchmarks, Fable 5.2 is smarter. But graphically I think this did a lot better job. I of course ran it through Busi bench as well and Gemini four Carbon actually came in second place. And when I look at these side by side, I actually think it should be the winner, but my LLM is a judge ranked this one second. And when we look at it, it took 11 minutes to generate but only 46 cents. Fable 5.2 cost $5. So I mean, don't be sleeping on Gemini four Carbon. It's a good model. It just got overshadowed by Fable 5.2 and some Jensen drama. Google also put out another model this week called Gemini 4 Hydrogen. And this is a smaller, faster, cheaper model. So this one's not going to win every single benchmark. Definitely not the benchmarks that are like the frontier level benchmarks. However, it is designed to be quite a bit less expensive. It's been being compared to the sort of like mid tier class models. But it is still apparently a pretty solid model, which is, you know, roughly as smart as Sonnet 5.5 but a bit cheaper and faster. In fact, according to this chart, quite a bit cheaper. And when we look down here, the average cost per task on its highest level is about $3.16 compared to Opus's $10.04. All right, those are the main stories of the week, but like every week, I do have a lot more that I do want to share. So let's jump into rapid fire. So this week was Adobe MAX out in Florida. So they're really leaning into this agent stuff where you can get into any one of the Adobe products, ask it questions, tell it what you want it to do, and it's just going to use their tools for you instead of you having to do all the clicking around and using the tools. They also showed off this Firefly design, which is very similar, like set up artwork for a musical festival using my assets. They upload a bunch of assets and then it goes and makes a bunch of flyers and things like that for you. Layout art boards for social media sizes. It goes and resizes everything for social media. Describe what you want, make the leather blue, changes the leather to blue. This is all Firefly video right now. So just a lot more like typing to get what you want as opposed to actually using the tools the old fashioned way. You upload images, you explain what you want, and then it goes and does the stuff for you. And pretty much all of the examples that I've seen so far to come out of Adobe Max have been this kind of thing where you're just editing stuff by typing and clicking and dragging. So, yeah, I think that's kind of the main takeaway from Adobe Max. Now, during the Adobe Max event every year, they do this thing called Sneaks, which is like their sneak preview of some of the stuff they're working on, but you don't get access to yet. So, they're working on things like being able to change perspective from one photo. So, you give it an original photo and then can have it give you a new camera pose, which is interesting cuz I feel like this is something we can already do with like GPT images and some of the other image tools that exist. They have this like Project Sound Bender where you can drag this thing around and change the sound that it's generating and sort of land on your ideal sound. Now, they did put out an exhaustive list of all the stuff that they showed off, and I'll put it down in the description. But if I'm being totally honest, most of it feels like stuff we've seen already, stuff we've seen out of OpenAI, stuff we've seen out of Runway, stuff we've seen out of a lot of other image and video platforms already. Now just kind of catching up and getting added inside of Adobe. Now, if you're a business, there's a new feature in ChatGPT that'll be pretty handy. It's called Businesses in ChatGPT, and this allows you to claim your business. So, it's kind of like like Google Shops where you can claim your store in Google, and if people search for your company and it pops up, you can kind of, you know, edit the store hours and all that kind of stuff. Well, Businesses in ChatGPT feels like something very similar. If people search out your business, you can claim that profile. You can get stats on how much that profile's being viewed and that sort of thing. But it also seems like you can edit details. So, you could sort of make sure it's accurately portraying your business the right way. Meta rolled out a new model this week called Muse Amber, which is a very small, efficient model, only 10 cents per million input tokens, 50 cents per million output tokens. You could see it's on par with like Haiku and Luna, actually a bit smarter, but roughly in the same cost range. Google also rolled out another model this week, the Gemini Decisions API. So like all of these companies have a Decisions API now. It started with Jev. We already talked about OpenAI's decision model earlier in this video. Microsoft has a Decisions model and well, now Google does too. We did get some additional news out of Anthropic this week. We got more details about their IPO. They're planning on offering it at between $70 and $78 per share and we got details about how many shares are going to be offered. No exact date yet though. We did get some new features in Claude though. We got Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors. Partners can now embed apps directly into Claude so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, Salesforce, NetSuite, Workday, things like that, but directly in line while you're inside of Claude. They have Claude Whiteboards, which is designed for sort of like brainstorming in like a whiteboard type environment. Claude Sheets, you can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, etc. Like it sounds like Claude has their own version of like Google Sheets or Excel built directly into Claude now. Claude Data, where you can connect it straight to your data and ask questions about your data. And they also introduced Claude Meetings, which if you can't tell by the title is pretty much a granola competitor. You jump on meetings, Claude will listen in on those meetings and take notes for you. You can also use your whiteboard directly inside of meetings and it's like this collaborative whiteboard thing inside of meetings, which seems pretty cool. I haven't actually tested this yet myself though. We got a new image model out of MiniMax this week. It can generate 4K images in just 10 seconds. It's called MiniMax H3 Image. It's available via API, MiniMax code, and on Hugging Face. There is a Hugging Face space available for this one so you can use it if you want and test it directly inside the Hugging Face platform. Here's some of their like pre-cached images that are already in here. A 1970s film frame of a woman waiting in the rainy Tokyo bus stop, isometric cutaway of a tiny underground bakery, a poster for a jazz festival in Lisbon. You know, it looks like a good image model. And finally, Automatic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coded apps amid a changing internet. So basically, Automatic is the company that makes WordPress. And now they're launching a new service called Space Fast. And Space Fast is essentially what Levable and Bolt and you know, a lot like these other app builder apps. You connect it to your favorite AI like ChatGPT, Claude Muse, Grokbot, Open Claude, whatever. And then you work inside of it to build whatever app you want to build. Again, not something I've tried myself, but something I'll probably test in the near future. And if it's really cool, I'll make another video about it. But that's what I got for you today. World-changing week, honestly. We have no clue what's going to happen with Nvidia. There's a lot up in the air as a result of all of the Jensen drama right now. Will it be good at convincing governments to, you know, help progress AI forward? All of this is up in the air. And honestly, I'm here for it all. Whether AI news accelerates and we get better and better and better models or AI comes to a halt, it still gives me interesting stuff to explore and talk about and try to help keep you in the loop. And that's what I do every week. I drink from the fire hose all week. I overwhelm myself, keep up with all the news, stay on top of everything, and then turn around and make a video a week at the end of the week, every Friday, that breaks down everything you need to know. I try to cut out all the fluff, all of the stuff that's overhyped that you don't really need to know about and share just the important stuff. And I record these on Thursday, so there could even be more news that comes out like late Thursday night or on Friday that I missed. If that happens, it'll make it into next Friday's video. I will make sure to keep you looped in. If you like that kind of stuff, make sure you like this video and subscribe to this channel and I will be sure to keep you looped in and on top of everything. Thank you so much for hanging out with me and nerding out with me today. Again, just such a wild, wild week. And uh yeah, I I I I don't know how this is going to play out, but we'll see. It'll be a fun ride. All right, thanks. See you in the next one. Bye-bye.

items.transcript: This is the biggest story in AI right now. Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and has been its only CEO for 33 years, just resigned after two weeks of reports about an affair and a woman that US intelligence thinks is a Chinese spy. I'm personally still in shock over this whole thing because Nvidia is at the center of the entire AI race. They make the chips most of this stuff runs on, and pretty much every company doing anything in AI is tied to Nvidia in some way. So let me walk you through it all. About a year ago, the US and Singapore confirmed they were investigating a company called MegaSpeed over whether Nvidia chips were getting around the export ban and into China. And one of its executives was a woman named Alice Huang, who's not related to Jensen. Then on October 29th, the New York Times reported that two of them had a close relationship, and Nvidia said that it was all just part of, you know, being a CEO. Then a week later, House Committee Chairman asked Jensen for a closed-door briefing, and the Times reported on a secret government memo calling her a spy for China's Ministry of State Security. Then this past Sunday, Jensen sent a letter to his whole company admitting he was unfaithful to his wife. Now, he didn't name anybody, but the same letter says that the board opened an independent investigation into the national security concerns. Then the information reported that companies tied to her and her family helped move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. And then yesterday, the Times reported another affair, this time with a vice president at Nvidia who reported directly to Jensen. Now, nobody involved has confirmed that one, but the Wall Street Journal reported the board was getting ready to push him out. And then this morning, Nvidia announced that he had resigned effective immediately without giving any more reason. Their CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO, and at one point this morning, the stock was down over 13%. Now, the spy allegations haven't been proven yet. China is calling it a smear, and Nvidia's board said it has no reason to believe any secrets got out. But personally, I'm pretty shocked by all of this and, I mean, a little sad too, because I really looked up to Jensen and so did a lot of people. So how this all played out has been super disappointing. But this does feel like history in the making right now because so much of where AI is headed had this one guy at the center of all of it. So the whole AI timeline from here feels a lot less certain than it did just a month ago. I recommend sharing this with a friend who follows AI or owns NVIDIA stock. And make sure you click that follow button to stay looped in with all the latest AI news and coolest tech every day.

items.title: How To Build An AI Operating System For Your Life
items.summary:
What if you could use AI agents to manage your emails, organize your schedule, create content, and help run your entire business?

I sat down with Peter Yang to explore the personal AI system he uses to run his one-person business. He walks me through his AI chief of staff, a personal advisor that keeps him focused on his goals, and the automated workflows he uses for podcast research, video editing, content creation, and everyday tasks.

We dive into how he connects ChatGPT, Claude Code, and GroqBot using reusable AI skills, how he keeps those skills improving over time, and how you can build your own versions of these workflows. I also walk through setting up a few of these automations myself so you can follow along.

Check out Peter Yang for more AI workflows, and explore his courses and AI skills at Behind the Craft:
🎬YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/@PeterYangYT
💻Behind the Craft: https://behindthecraft.com


Sharing the latest news and advancements in AI

🛠️ Explor

items.transcript: So, this might be the coolest thing you see today. Ring, the doorbell company, just made a security camera that flies around your house all on its own, and it's only 250 bucks. It's called the Ring Drone Cam, and this is the actual thing flying around at its launch event. It sits in a little dock, and when one of your Ring sensors goes off, it takes off by itself, flies over to check it out, and then streams what it sees directly to your phone. So, you don't need a camera in every single room of your house. Now, Ring actually announced this back in 2020, but it never shipped because every time they added more sensors and computing power, it just got heavier and heavier, which, you know, made it fly worse. And the developers said that with all that was in it, it was going to cost like 5 grand. So, they basically took the entire brain out of it and put it in the cloud instead. The drone just flies, streams video, and lands. And a system they call AI Pilot does the navigating over your own Wi-Fi, which is how this thing ended up lighter than most phones. Now, to set it up, you just carry it around your house once, and it maps it all out, building a floor plan and then suggesting spots to patrol. Now, it only flies for up to 8 minutes and then needs about an hour to go recharge itself afterwards, which, you know, probably not ideal, but you know, this is V1. They also claim that it's loud on purpose, so whoever broke in hears it coming. And another thing to note is the camera is always off while it's docked, so it's not watching things while it's sitting in its dock. And that AI Pilot that I just mentioned, it's already driving this $1,000 robot for businesses. It uses this camera that pops up like 4 ft like a periscope. The drone ships January 27th, assuming the FCC clears it all, which only makes it about 6 years late, but still cool nonetheless. So, share this with your friend who loves home gadgets and drones, and don't forget to click that follow button to see the coolest tech every single day.

items.transcript: This might be the coolest thing you're going to see today. Boston Dynamics took the feet off of their humanoid Atlas robot and added wheels. And now it's drifting around the warehouse and doing 360 spins on what are probably the most expensive roller skates ever made. And this is the real robot. It's not a render. And the only new part that they built was one adapter that connects an off-the-shelf scooter rim to its ankle motor. And the way they got it moving is actually really clever. They told the robot that each wheel is just an ankle that keeps on spinning. And then they let it practice in a simulation millions of times. So nobody actually programmed this rolling. It figured it out on its own. And here's that 360 which came from a motion capture of a real person jumping. And it worked on the real robot on the very first try. And my favorite is these side dashes where a person would slide their feet, but the robot figured out it should just steer the wheels and roll through it instead. Now the engineer behind it, Andy Wu, drives it around with a game controller. And he says he hasn't even touched his gaming rig since they built this, which is probably a pretty strong recruitment pitch. And the wheels, they were just a way to try to push the Atlas motors to their limits since they are spinning fast under load the whole time. And then what they learned goes back into the actual Atlas robot that, you know, still has feet, which by the way is also the one that Hyundai wants to put into their car factories in 2028. I don't know. I think it's pretty sweet to see this humanoid robot skating around like it's a hockey player or something. But if you think it's cool too, share it with your friends who love robots.
